result.verdict: The tracking, gate docking and captions mostly hold up. The rollout section is spoiled by long cross-dissolves that show the same 787 twice. The high aerial taxi shots have no aircraft shadow, look washed out and have jagged dark strips on the ground. Smaller problems: caption timing and framing.

findings.issue: Both rollout-section samples land in the middle of a cross-dissolve between two shots of the same aircraft, so the 787 appears twice. In arr_04 a translucent second 'UNITED' title, a second fin and two large see-through discs sit over the rolling aircraft. The discs are the head-on engine faces from the touchdown shot and read as ghost wheels. In arr_05 a ghost fin and nacelle sit to the right of the aircraft, and a huge translucent dark curved shape covers the left half of the frame (the next shot's taxiway). Two of 14 evenly spaced samples hit a dissolve, which suggests the dissolves last about 1.5-2 s. Because the subject sits in nearly the same place in both shots, the overlap reads as a render glitch, not a transition. Neither frame has a caption or badge, so no rollout label is ever seen.
findings.fix: Use hard cuts, or dissolves of 0.3-0.5 s at most, between consecutive shots of the same aircraft (touchdown to rollout, rollout to taxi). Alternatively dip through black or white, or make sure the subject's screen position and scale differ enough that the overlap does not look like a doubled aircraft. Keep the phase label visible across the transition so the rollout shot clearly shows 'Rollout'.

findings.issue: In the high aerial taxi shots the aircraft casts no visible ground shadow, although the lighting is a low late-afternoon sun. In arr_08 the white 787 sits on light-beige concrete with nothing beneath or beside it and seems to hover. arr_07 shows the same on the light concrete under the tail and wing. The shadow returns once the camera is lower (arr_09 to arr_13). The likely cause is shadow-map or cascade range or resolution dropping out at camera altitude, not cloud shading.
findings.fix: Extend the shadow cascade or far distance for these camera heights, or fit the shadow camera tightly around the tracked aircraft. As a fallback, add a soft contact or blob shadow under the aircraft when the shadow map cannot resolve it.

findings.issue: Two dark strips on the infield, at x~300 y 255-515 and x~720-800 y 425-540, with red and white dots inside, have heavily stair-stepped, pixelated edges. They look like a low-resolution raster mask stretched over the ground and are an obvious artifact from this altitude. The dark diagonal bands at upper left look the same.
findings.fix: Rebuild these road or retired-pavement strips as vector polygons, or use a higher-resolution or filtered mask, so the edges are straight and anti-aliased.

findings.issue: Thin dark-grey stroke patterns on the beige infield (a rectangle with branching lines, odd letter-like shapes) look like a schematic map drawn on the ground rather than real service roads or pavement. This is separate from the known flat infield texture.
findings.fix: Give the service roads or retired pavement a believable width, edge and material, or remove them if they are leftover data outlines.

findings.issue: The aerial taxi shots are washed out and almost monochrome beige. Apron, taxiway, infield and the white aircraft have very little contrast, and the low haze or flat exposure makes the subject hard to pick out, especially in arr_08.
findings.fix: Lower exposure or haze for high-altitude cameras, or add a mild contrast or saturation grade to these shots, so the pavement reads darker than the infield and the aircraft stands out.

findings.issue: This frame has no phase label and no time-lapse badge, although it falls inside the time-lapsed taxi sequence (6x in arr_06, 8x in arr_08). A viewer cannot tell the speed is altered. Two near-identical United widebodies are also in frame with nothing marking which one is UAL900.
findings.fix: Keep the speed badge on screen for the whole time any time-lapse plays. Mark the subject, for example with a small callsign tag, or frame so the second United aircraft does not compete.

findings.issue: An airfield sign seen from behind (blank beige board on two posts) sits in the extreme lower-left corner, cut by the frame edge and touching the 'Touchdown, runway 28R' caption, so it reads as stray geometry. The caption already says 'Touchdown' while the aircraft is still about 20 m up. From this ground-level infield camera, runway 28R under the aircraft is not readable, only a thin grey band at the horizon, so the 787 appears to descend onto a beige field.
findings.fix: Move the camera a few metres so the sign is out of frame or clearly placed, and raise the camera or shift it laterally so the runway surface under the flare path is visible. Alternatively, delay the 'Touchdown' caption until the wheels are near the ground.

findings.issue: The 'Final approach' shot looks straight up at the aircraft against an empty sky with no ground or runway reference. The nose-up attitude seen from below reads more like a takeoff climb than a descent to 28R.
findings.fix: Include some ground, the shoreline or the approach lights in frame, or use a side-on or chase angle that shows the descent path.

findings.issue: The cloud layer below the camera is drawn as flat white blotches on both the bay and the distant land, with no volume or shadows. It reads like foam or snow patches pasted on the ground. Thirty seconds later (arr_02) the same clouds sit above the aircraft. The third title line ('Followed from the bay to the gate · recorded ADS-B, 8 Nov 2026') is very small light-grey text on a pale sky and is barely legible.
findings.fix: Soften or give volume to low cloud sprites, or start the title shot below the cloud base for consistency. Enlarge the third title line or raise its contrast, for example with a darker scrim behind the title block.

findings.issue: The hangar or large building behind the runway is a plain light-grey box with no openings and dark smudges on one face. It reads as placeholder geometry. Similar untextured white boxes appear in the aerial shots.
findings.fix: Give these hangars a basic facade texture (door panels, roof edge, a little colour variation), or keep them out of the hero framing.

findings.issue: The aircraft's fin, tail and aft fuselage are cut off at the left frame edge while about 40% of the frame shows empty apron and building at right.
findings.fix: Pan or zoom out slightly so the whole aircraft, or at least the fin, stays in frame as it turns into G7.

findings.issue: The dark asphalt taxiway ends along a long straight diagonal edge (about (300,265) to (210,445)). Yellow taxi centrelines continue onto a lighter mottled surface with green blotches beyond it, which looks like a pavement tile or polygon cut off rather than a deliberate asphalt-to-concrete change. Low confidence.
findings.fix: Check the pavement polygon or texture tile at this location. If it is a real asphalt/concrete joint, blend the shade change or align it with the real pavement edge.

result.verdict: Strong aircraft model, gate and runway work, with clean captions. The ending is weak: the last climb-out shot skims featureless desert-looking terrain at ridge height, the climb-out terrain has a visible pit artifact, and there are several smaller texture, sky and transition flaws.

findings.issue: The final climb-out shot puts the camera a few metres above the hills. The lower ~45% of the frame is a blurry, low-resolution beige surface with soft dune-like lumps and no vegetation, roads or houses, so it reads as a desert rather than the San Bruno and Sweeney Ridge hills. Flat grey rectangles at left (0-350, 295-345) look like un-extruded building footprints. The sea horizon sits at y~245 and the 777 spans y~235-290, at or below the camera's height and level with the ridge line, so it looks like the jet is terrain-skimming about 24 s after rotation. The aircraft is also small (~130 px wide).
findings.fix: Raise the chase camera well above the terrain (keep it above both the aircraft and the ridge, or fix it to an altitude band over the DEM), or shoot from a higher, farther angle. Use the terrain imagery and texture tier (not the flat fallback) for the peninsula hills, or end the film on dep_12's framing over the suburbs.

findings.issue: Terrain artifact in the San Bruno suburbs at about (640-710, 338-362): a dark pit whose walls show vertically smeared, streaked texture. It looks like a DEM no-data hole or a tile skirt rather than a real feature.
findings.fix: Fill or clamp the DEM hole (nodata to neighbour interpolation) and/or hide tile skirts at that LOD.

findings.issue: This mid-film transition is a long cross-dissolve between two taxi shots. It produces a double exposure: a large, half-transparent side view of the 777 (UNITED titles, engine) sits over a top-down 777 on the same frame, and a big dark wedge from the other shot lies across the apron like a giant shadow. The 'Taxi to runway 28R' caption and the time-lapse badge both drop out, although the phase is the same before (dep_03) and after (dep_05).
findings.fix: Use a hard cut or a short (<0.5 s) dissolve between same-phase shots. Keep the phase caption on screen across the transition and only cross-fade the badge value (3x to 12x).

findings.issue: The hillside band behind the taxiing aircraft shows a row of blank, uniform pale-grey trapezoids with crisp edges and curved roads drawn over them (x 60-650, y 135-195). They read as untextured landuse fills, possibly the Golden Gate National Cemetery or big parking lots. The same patches are visible behind the runway in dep_10_t120.5.png (x 130-330, y 195-220).
findings.fix: Give those landuse polygons a proper texture (lawn plus headstone or stall pattern) or let the base imagery show through instead of a flat fill.

findings.issue: Each wing has an opaque dark-blue diamond-shaped blob about 2-3 m inboard of the tip. In the rear view the wing visibly continues past it to the white rear position light. The same blob shows at the wingtips in dep_03, dep_08, dep_09, dep_11 and dep_13. A United 777-300ER wing has no blue feature there (nav lights are red and green), so it looks like fin-blue paint mapped onto a tip fairing, or a leftover tip from the shorter base wing.
findings.fix: Check the atlas or paint of the wingtip and raked-tip region on the 777-300ER model. Remove the blue patch or turn it into correctly coloured, small nav-light lenses at the true tip.

findings.issue: Seen from astern or rear-quarter, the vertical fin reads white or pale grey (also in dep_10_t120.5.png, dep_13_t156.0.png, and largely white in dep_03_t37.5.png). The United fin and rudder are blue on both sides, and dep_09 shows the blue globe fin correctly. The rudder or trailing-edge region may be unpainted, or specular light washes it out. Low confidence.
findings.fix: Check the fin trailing-edge and rudder UVs and paint on the 777 bake. Make sure the blue covers the rudder and the fin's trailing edge.

findings.issue: The caption says 'Pushback' (5x TIME-LAPSE) while the aircraft is still at the stand with two bridges docked at doors 1L and 2L. Bridges retract before a push, so the label runs ahead of what is shown.
findings.fix: Start the 'Pushback' caption when the bridges have retracted and the aircraft starts moving, or label the lead-in 'At gate G13 / Bridges retracting'.

findings.issue: In the 'Lining up, runway 28R' side view, the main and nose gear touch the far edge of the dark pavement band (y~268). The white runway dashes sit well in front (y~287-300). By perspective the aircraft does not read as being on the centreline and looks close to the far edge.
findings.fix: Check the lateral position against the 28R centreline at this time (ADS-B snap or offset). If it is correct, choose a camera angle that makes the centreline position clear.

findings.issue: The sky has an olive/khaki cast (sampled ~RGB 214,214,188 in dep_07, dep_08 and dep_11) with flat, darker-grey cloud strokes that have no sunlit side. In late-afternoon light, clouds should be lit warm or white, not dark smudges. Seen in dep_03, 06, 07, 08, 09, 11 and 12.
findings.fix: Add some blue back into the sky dome away from the sun, and shade the cloud layer with the sun direction (lit tops and edges, warm tint) instead of a constant darker grey.

findings.issue: Take-off chase framing: the camera is so close behind the tailplane that the vertical fin is cut off by the top edge of the frame. The aircraft body sits in the lower middle with half the frame given to the runway surface.
findings.fix: Pull the camera back or up by about 10-15 m, or widen the FOV, so the full fin is in frame.

findings.issue: An elevated AirTrain-style guideway rises from the lower left and ends abruptly in mid-air over a parking lot, with a single car parked on its end at about (785,460). No station building surrounds it (the RCC station looks culled at this distance).
findings.fix: Keep the RCC station or terminus building in this LOD and distance tier, or cull the guideway and car together with it.

findings.issue: Isolated red-outlined squares are scattered across the open apron (e.g. (380,298), (483,343), (590,422), (686,392), (709,425), (855,406)), well away from the aircraft. They may be hydrant-pit outlines, but at this scale they read like debug markers. The 'DEPARTURE' kicker in thin orange letter-spaced caps also has low contrast against the hazy beige background.
findings.fix: Confirm the squares are intended hydrant-pit markings and tone them down (thinner or less saturated), or drop them. Add a subtle dark gradient behind the title block for contrast.
